OpenDataLoader PDF

 PDF Parser for AI-ready data. Automate PDF accessibility. Open-source. 

 
 
 
 
 

 

🔍 PDF parser for AI data extraction — Extract Markdown, JSON (with bounding boxes), and HTML from any PDF. 1 in benchmarks (0.907 overall). Deterministic local mode + AI hybrid mode for complex pages.

- How accurate is it? — 1 in benchmarks: 0.907 overall, 0.928 table accuracy across 200 real-world PDFs including multi-column and scientific papers. Deterministic local mode + AI hybrid mode for complex pages (benchmarks)
- Scanned PDFs and OCR? — Yes. Built-in OCR (80+ languages) in hybrid mode. Works with poor-quality scans at 300 DPI+ (hybrid mode)
- Tables, formulas, images, charts? — Yes. Complex/borderless tables, LaTeX formulas, and AI-generated picture/chart descriptions all via hybrid mode (hybrid mode)
- How do I use this for RAG? — pip install opendataloader-pdf , convert in 3 lines. Outputs structured Markdown for chunking, JSON with bounding boxes for source citations, and HTML. LangChain integration available. Python, Node.js, Java SDKs (quick start LangChain)

♿ PDF accessibility automation — Auto-tag untagged PDFs into screen-reader-ready Tagged PDFs at scale. First open-source tool to generate Tagged PDFs end-to-end.

- What's the problem? — Accessibility regulations are now enforced worldwide. Manual PDF remediation costs $50–200 per document and doesn't scale (regulations)
- What's free? — Layout analysis + auto-tagging (Apache 2.0). Untagged PDF in → Tagged PDF out. No proprietary SDK dependency (auto-tagging)
- What about PDF/UA compliance? — Converting Tagged PDF to PDF/UA-1 or PDF/UA-2 is an enterprise add-on. Auto-tagging generates the Tagged PDF; PDF/UA export is the final step (pipeline)
- Why trust this? — Built in collaboration with Dual Lab (veraPDF developers) based on PDF Association specifications, best practice guides and expertise of the PDF Community. Auto-tagging follows the Well-Tagged PDF specification, validated with veraPDF (collaboration)

 Get Started in 30 Seconds

 Requires : Java 11+ and Python 3.11+ (Node.js Java also available)

 Before you start: run java -version . If not found, install JDK 11+ from Adoptium.

 

 

 

 Annotated PDF output — each element (heading, paragraph, table, image) detected with bounding boxes and semantic type.

install.title: Get Started in 30 Seconds
install.html:
Requires: Java 11+ and Python 3.11+ (Node.js | Java also available)

Before you start: run java -version. If not found, install JDK 11+ from Adoptium.

pip install -U opendataloader-pdf

import opendataloader_pdf

# Batch all files in one call — each convert() spawns a JVM process, so repeated calls are slow
opendataloader_pdf.convert(
    input_path=["file1.pdf", "file2.pdf", "folder/"],
    output_dir="output/",
    format="markdown,json"
)

{
  "type": "heading",
  "id": 42,
  "level": "Title",
  "page number": 1,
  "bounding box": [72.0, 700.0, 540.0, 730.0],
  "heading level": 1,
  "font": "Helvetica-Bold",
  "font size": 24.0,
  "text color": "[0.0]",
  "content": "Introduction"
}
Field Description
type Element type: heading, paragraph, table, list, image, caption, formula, form field
id Unique identifier for cross-referencing
page number 1-indexed page reference
bounding box [left, bottom, right, top] in PDF points (72pt = 1 inch)
heading level Heading depth (1+)
content Extracted text
field role, checked Form field (tagged PDF with --use-struct-tree): check box or radio button; on, off, or neutral

Full JSON Schema

features.title: Advanced Features
features.html:
Tagged PDF Support

When a PDF has structure tags, OpenDataLoader extracts the exact layout the author intended — no guessing, no heuristics. Headings, lists, tables, and reading order are preserved from the source. Printed check boxes and radio buttons (Form elements with PrintField attributes) become form field elements in JSON and task list items (- [x], - [ ]) in Markdown.

Output quality depends on tag quality. Not all tagged PDFs are well-tagged. For PDFs with sparse or incorrect tags, the default heuristic mode or --hybrid docling-fast often produces better results.

--use-struct-tree takes precedence over --hybrid. If both are set on a tagged PDF, the structure tree is used and the hybrid backend is not called (a well-tagged PDF already carries reading order and structure). Drop --use-struct-tree if you want the hybrid backend instead.

# Batch all files in one call — each convert() spawns a JVM process, so repeated calls are slow
opendataloader_pdf.convert(
    input_path=["file1.pdf", "file2.pdf", "folder/"],
    output_dir="output/",
    use_struct_tree=True           # Use native PDF structure tags
)

Most PDF parsers ignore structure tags entirely. Learn more

AI Safety: Prompt Injection Protection

PDFs can contain hidden prompt injection attacks. OpenDataLoader automatically filters:

  • Hidden text (transparent, zero-size fonts)
  • Off-page content
  • Suspicious invisible layers

To sanitize sensitive data (emails, URLs, phone numbers → placeholders), enable it explicitly:

# Batch all files in one call — each invocation spawns a JVM process, so repeated calls are slow
opendataloader-pdf file1.pdf file2.pdf folder/ --sanitize
Custom Sanitization Rules

To use your own rules, give a JSON rules file with --sanitize-rules (Python: sanitize_rules, Node.js: sanitizeRules). This option also turns on --sanitize. Only the rules of the file run, in place of the built-in rules.

{
  "rules": [
    { "id": "kr-mobile", "pattern": "(?<!\\d)01[016789]-\\d{3,4}-\\d{4}(?!\\d)", "replacement": "010-0000-0000" }
  ]
}

opendataloader-pdf file1.pdf folder/ --sanitize-rules rules.json

To keep the built-in rules, start from examples/sanitize-rules/default-rules.json. It has the built-in rules of --sanitize. Copy it, then add, change, or delete rules. If a later release changes the built-in rules, compare your copy with the new template.

Each rule has three keys:

Key Value
id 1 to 64 characters from a-z, 0-9, and -. Each ID only once
pattern A Java regular expression, 1 to 5,000 characters
replacement Literal text, 1 to 200 characters, with no control characters ($1 is not a group reference)

The run stops before any file is processed if the rules file has one of these problems:

  • An unknown or missing key, or a value of the wrong type.
  • A rule ID that is repeated or has a wrong format.
  • A pattern that is empty or does not compile, or a replacement that is empty or has a control character.
  • A value over a limit: a file larger than 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes), more than 200 rules, or a pattern or replacement that is too long.
  • No rules.

The error gives the reason, and the rule or the key.

How the rules work:

  • All rules run on the original text of each line. A match cannot cross a line, and a rule does not see the placeholder of another rule.
  • If two matches overlap, the match that starts first is kept. If they start at the same position, the longer match is kept. If they also have the same length, the match of the earlier rule in the file is kept.
  • Rules apply to the extracted text. They do not apply to image descriptions, formulas, or document metadata such as the title.

Warning: A pattern runs on every text line, with no time limit. Some patterns are very slow, also on a short line. For example, nested repetition with limits such as (a{1,20}){1,20}$ can take tens of seconds on a line of 31 characters, and the time grows fast with the length of the line. Some patterns overflow the stack on a long line, for example (a|b)*c. Then that file fails with an error that names the rule, and the run continues with the next file. Use only rules files that you trust. Test each new pattern on lines as long as your real text.

\w matches only ASCII letters, digits, and _. On Java 19 and later, \b uses the same ASCII rule. On Java 11 to 18, \b also counts other letters, such as Hangul, as word characters. Use (?<!\d) and (?!\d) around numbers.

AI Safety Guide

LangChain Integration
pip install -U langchain-opendataloader-pdf

from langchain_opendataloader_pdf import OpenDataLoaderPDFLoader

loader = OpenDataLoaderPDFLoader(
    file_path=["file1.pdf", "file2.pdf", "folder/"],
    format="text"
)
documents = loader.load()

Advanced Options
# Batch all files in one call — each convert() spawns a JVM process, so repeated calls are slow
opendataloader_pdf.convert(
    input_path=["file1.pdf", "file2.pdf", "folder/"],
    output_dir="output/",
    format="json,markdown,pdf",
    image_output="embedded",        # "off", "embedded" (Base64), or "external" (default)
    image_format="jpeg",            # "png" or "jpeg"
    use_struct_tree=True,           # Use native PDF structure
)

Full CLI Options Reference

PDF Bytes In, String Out

Convert a PDF that you have in memory, and get the output as a string:

markdown = opendataloader_pdf.convert_bytes(pdf_bytes)                   # format="markdown" (default)
json_text = opendataloader_pdf.convert_bytes(pdf_bytes, format="json", password="...")

import { convertBytes } from '@opendataloader/pdf';

const markdown = await convertBytes(pdfBuffer);                     // format: 'markdown' (default)
const jsonText = await convertBytes(pdfBuffer, { format: 'json', pages: '1-3' });
  • One format for each call: markdown, text, json, or html. The other options of convert() apply, except the output folder, to_stdout, and the image folder.
  • Images are off by default. Use image_output="embedded" (imageOutput: 'embedded') for Base64 images.
  • The bytes go to a private temporary file, which is removed after the call. Each call starts one Java process: for many files, convert() with a list of paths is faster.
  • For a file, convert(..., format="markdown", to_stdout=True) (toStdout: true) also returns the output as a string.
